    Building a Repository and Managing Environments

    Last updated on 2026-11-03 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What actually belongs in a code repository?
    • Why does each project need its own environment?
    • How do I turn mooring_tools/ into something pip install-able?

    Objectives

    • Create a project with uv and lay out a repository with a src/ package, notebooks, and data kept separate
    • Add dependencies to a project and explain what pyproject.toml and uv.lock each record
    • Run a Jupyter notebook inside the project’s environment and import your own package from it
    • Explain why a src/ layout catches packaging bugs that a flat layout hides

    What goes in a repo

    By the end of Block 2, mooring_tools/ is three modules and an __init__.py, sitting next to first_analysis.ipynb. That’s enough to import from this notebook. It’s not enough to share with a colleague, or use from a notebook anywhere else on your machine. For that, the package needs a proper home:

    gs01sumo-mooring-tools/
├── .gitignore
├── .python-version
├── LICENSE
├── README.md
├── pyproject.toml
├── uv.lock
├── src/
│   └── mooring_tools/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       ├── stats.py
│       ├── plotting.py
│       └── merge.py
├── notebooks/
│   └── first_analysis.ipynb
└── data/
    ├── gi01sumo_nsif_ctd.nc
    └── gi01sumo_nsif_dosta.nc

    A few things to note about the layout:

    • src/mooring_tools/, not just mooring_tools/ as the repo root.
    • notebooks/ and data/ are separate from the package. The package is code meant to be imported; the notebook is one particular analysis that uses it.
    • pyproject.toml and uv.lock describe the project and the exact packages it was run with. Both are committed. We’ll build them up over this block.
    • .python-version records which version of Python the project is developed with.
    • .gitignore keeps generated/environment files out of version control, such as the venv folder, __pycache__/, and Jupyter checkpoint files.
    • LICENSE states what others are allowed to do with the code.

    Creating the project with uv

    You could create all of that by hand. Instead, we’ll let uv create the skeleton. uv is one tool that replaces several you may have used separately: it installs Python itself, creates virtual environments, installs packages, and records what it installed. Confirm it’s available:

    BASH 

    uv --version

    Then create the project:

    BASH 

    uv init --lib --name mooring-tools gi01sumo-mooring-tools
    • --lib asks for a library layout: a src/ folder with a package inside it, ready to be imported by other code.
    • --name mooring-tools is the name the project is installed under. The folder is named gi01sumo-mooring-tools, so we give the name explicitly.
    • uv also runs git init for you, so the folder is already a repository.
    Callout

    Two names for one thing

    The project is called mooring-tools (with a hyphen) but you import it as mooring_tools (with an underscore). The first is the name used to install and publish it; the second is a Python identifier, so it can’t contain a hyphen. uv turns one into the other automatically. If you see ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'mooring-tools', that’s the mix-up.

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: Lay out the repository

    1. Run the uv init command above, then cd into the new folder and look at what it created (ls -a, or dir on Windows).
    2. uv init puts a placeholder hello() function in src/mooring_tools/__init__.py. Replace that file with your __init__.py from Block 2, and move stats.py, plotting.py, and merge.py into src/mooring_tools/.
    3. Create notebooks/ and data/, and move first_analysis.ipynb and the two .nc files into them. (Update the data paths in the notebook to ../data/....)

    Why src/, specifically

    Compare two layouts, both without the package actually installed:

    BASH 

    # flat layout: mooring_tools/ directly at the repo root
cd flat-layout-repo
python3 -c "import mooring_tools"

    OUTPUT 

    (imports successfully — from mooring_tools/__init__.py right there in the folder)

    BASH 

    # src layout: mooring_tools/ inside src/
cd src-layout-repo
python3 -c "import mooring_tools"

    OUTPUT 

    ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'mooring_tools'

    With a flat layout, Python finds the package because your current directory is always searched first. That means import mooring_tools can silently “work” from inside the repo even if the package was never actually installed, or if the install is broken. The bug only shows up later, when someone tries to use the package from outside the repo and it’s nowhere to be found. With src/, that failure happens immediately.

    Environments

    Every Python installation on your machine has one set of installed packages by default. If two projects need different, incompatible versions of the same library, installing globally means only one project can work at a time. A virtual environment gives each project its own isolated set of installed packages.

    With uv you don’t create or activate one yourself. The first time you add a dependency (next section), uv creates a .venv folder in the project and installs into it. Every uv run ... command then uses that environment automatically, from the project folder or any folder inside it. There is no activate step to forget, and no way to install into the wrong environment by accident.

    Callout

    The .venv folder is disposable

    Nothing in .venv is precious. If it ever gets into a confusing state, delete the folder and run uv sync. uv will rebuild it from the project files. That is also why .venv is in .gitignore: it’s machine-specific, and fully recreatable.

    Making the package installable

    pyproject.toml (Tom’s Obvious Minimal Language), at the repo root, is what turns a src/ folder into something pip understands:

    TOML 

    [project]
name = "mooring-tools"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
authors = [
    { name = "Your Name", email = "you@example.org" }
]
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = []

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.11.32,<0.12.0"]
build-backend = "uv_build"

    Two things need your attention before we go on. (Your version numbers and author will differ.)

    • requires-python defaults to the version of Python uv found on your machine. If yours is 3.14, a colleague on 3.11 would be told they cannot install your package, for no real reason. Our code runs fine on older versions, so relax it to ">=3.10".
    • description should say what the package does. Make it "Burst-statistics, plotting, and merge utilities for OOI GS01SUMO CTD/DOSTA data".

    The [build-system] table tells tools how to turn src/ into an installable package. uv fills it in; you don’t need to edit it.

    Adding dependencies

    Our code needs xarray, netCDF4, pandas, numpy, and matplotlib. Add them with:

    BASH 

    uv add xarray netcdf4 pandas numpy matplotlib

    That one command does three things:

    1. creates .venv if it doesn’t exist yet,
    2. installs the packages (and everything they depend on) into it
    3. records them in two places.

    Look at pyproject.toml again:

    TOML 

    dependencies = [
    "matplotlib>=3.10.9",
    "netcdf4>=1.7.3",
    "numpy>=2.2.6",
    "pandas>=2.3.3",
    "xarray>=2025.6.1",
]

    uv has written a minimum version for each one: the version it installed, or the oldest version that works with the oldest Python you allow. This says what your code needs to run at all, loose enough not to fight with other projects.

    For notebooks, add JupyterLab as a development dependency. This is something you need to work on the project, but that someone else who is only using mooring_tools does not:

    BASH 

    uv add --dev jupyterlab

    TOML 

    [dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "jupyterlab>=4.6.5",
]
    Challenge

    Challenge 2: Set up the project’s dependencies

    In the project folder, fix requires-python and description in pyproject.toml, then run both uv add commands above. Open pyproject.toml and confirm the dependencies and [dependency-groups] tables were filled in for you. Which new files and folders has uv created?

    .venv/ (the environment, git-ignored) and uv.lock (the exact record of what was installed, which we look at shortly). pyproject.toml itself was edited by uv add.

    Your minimum versions will differ from the ones above, because they reflect whatever was current when you ran the command.

    Running code in the project

    To run a command inside the project’s environment, put uv run in front of it:

    BASH 

    uv run python -c "import mooring_tools; print(mooring_tools.__file__)"

    The printed path should point into your repo’s src/mooring_tools/. uv installs your own package into .venv in editable mode: Python imports it directly from your src/ files rather than from a copy, so edits you make take effect immediately without reinstalling (This is the persistent cousin of Block 2’s %autoreload).

    Now start JupyterLab inside the project:

    BASH 

    uv run jupyter lab

    Open notebooks/first_analysis.ipynb. The notebook’s kernel is the project’s .venv Python, so import mooring_tools simply works.

    Challenge

    Challenge 3: Use the package from a notebook

    Launch JupyterLab with uv run jupyter lab from the repo root. In a new notebook inside notebooks/, run:

    PYTHON 

    import mooring_tools
from mooring_tools.stats import resample_burst_stats
print(mooring_tools.__file__)

    Then change the body of a function in src/mooring_tools/stats.py (for example, the default freq), and call it again. Do you need to restart the kernel? (Remember what %autoreload 2 did in Block 2.)

    The printed path points at your repo’s src/mooring_tools/. Whether the edit shows up without a restart depends on whether you ran %load_ext autoreload and %autoreload 2: the editable install makes the package findable from anywhere, while autoreload makes already-imported code refresh in a running kernel.

    If import mooring_tools raises ModuleNotFoundError, the notebook is almost certainly running in a different Python than the project’s. Check that you started JupyterLab with uv run jupyter lab, not with a jupyter installed elsewhere on your machine.

    Package management: the lock file

    pyproject.toml has loose, minimum versions. For exact reproducibility look at the other file uv created: uv.lock. It records the exact version of every package in the environment, including the ones you never asked for directly (xarray pulls in packaging, pandas pulls in python-dateutil, and so on):

    [[package]]
name = "xarray"
version = "2026.9.0"
...

    (You don’t write or edit uv.lock; uv maintains it every time you uv add, uv remove, or uv lock.)

    The difference between pyproject.toml and uv.lock is that the former declares what is needed to run your code whereas the latter states exactly what your environment has installed at the time that uv was run. installed, version by version. The lock file covers every platform and Python version your project supports, so a lock file made on a Mac works on Windows and Linux.

    Commit both files. Then reproducing your environment on a new machine is:

    BASH 

    git clone <repo-url>
cd gi01sumo-mooring-tools
uv sync

    uv sync creates .venv and installs exactly what uv.lock says. If the right Python isn’t installed on the new machine, uv downloads it too.

    Challenge

    Challenge 4: Reproduce your environment

    Commit your work (git add . then git commit). Then, in a different folder, clone your own repo and run uv sync. Compare the output of uv run python -c "import xarray; print(xarray.__version__)" in the clone and in your original. What do you expect?

    When that works, delete the .venv folder in your original project and run uv sync again. How long does it take compared to the first time?

    The versions match, because both environments were built from the same uv.lock.

    Rebuilding is much faster the second time: uv keeps a cache of everything it has already downloaded, so a rebuild is mostly linking files from that cache into a new .venv.

    Changing your mind later

    You’ll rarely get the dependency list right the first time. The same commands work whenever you need them:

    BASH 

    uv add scipy           # new dependency
uv remove scipy        # no longer needed
uv lock --upgrade      # move to the newest versions allowed, then...
uv sync                # ...bring .venv in line with uv.lock

    Each of these edits pyproject.toml and/or uv.lock for you, so the two files and the environment stay consistent. Commit the changed files together.

    Callout

    .gitignore and what to commit

    uv init already wrote a .gitignore containing .venv, __pycache__/, *.py[oc], build/, dist/, wheels/, and *.egg-info. Add one line for Jupyter:

    .ipynb_checkpoints/

    Commit: pyproject.toml, uv.lock, .python-version, README.md, LICENSE, and everything under src/ and notebooks/. Don’t commit .venv/.

    If your data files are large or sensitive, consider whether data/ belongs in .gitignore too, with a note in the README on where to get it.

    Callout

    What about conda?

    Many scientists use conda or mamba, and for good reason: it can install non-Python libraries (compilers, GDAL, and so on) that uv cannot. Every package in this workshop is available as a pre-built wheel for macOS, Windows, and Linux, so uv is enough here. If a future project needs non-Python system libraries, conda remains a sensible choice for that project. The ideas in this block — one environment per project, minimum versions in the project file, exact versions in a lock file, commit both — apply either way.

    Wrap-up

    By the end of this block, mooring_tools is a real, installable package: src/ layout, a pyproject.toml declaring what it needs, a uv.lock recording exactly what was installed, and an environment that uv builds and uses without any activation. A colleague can reproduce all of it with git clone and uv sync. Block 4 adds the README and docstring pass that makes this repo usable by someone who isn’t you.

    Key Points
    • Separate the installable package (src/mooring_tools/) from notebooks and data
    • A src/ layout turns “the package isn’t actually installed” from a silent bug into a raised error
    • uv init --lib creates the project skeleton; uv add installs a dependency and records it in pyproject.toml and uv.lock
    • uv run runs a command in the project’s environment with nothing to activate; the .venv folder is disposable and never committed
    • pyproject.toml declares what your code needs (minimum versions); uv.lock records exactly what’s installed: commit both, and reproduction is git clone plus uv sync
